subject: botany_2
question_text: What is green revolution? Who is regarded as the Father of the green revolution?

verification.note: Sourced from "Sr. Botany — My Baby Bullet-Q" (Sri Publishers, STAR-Q Pass Track), book p.46, printed question 124. Botany-II holds only ONE source book: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no Telangana Botany-II board paper is in the corpus, so the two-book union check and the board back-test are BOTH structurally impossible for this card — "not checked" does NOT mean "checked and clean". Run both the moment a second source or a real paper arrives. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Revised 2026-09-05: s2_who's first common mistake called a single name an error, although Norman Borlaug alone answers the question and the insider note says so, so the entry now warns about writing both names without labelling them.

insider_note: A definition and a name. Norman Borlaug is the world answer; if you add M. S. Swaminathan as the Indian one, say which is which.

steps.why: Semi-dwarf varieties could carry a heavy head of grain without falling over, which is what allowed heavy fertiliser use to translate into yield.
common_mistakes: Saying it was about growing more land area. It was about higher YIELD from the same land.
Leaving out high yielding varieties. They are the heart of the definition.

steps.margin_note: Both names, each labelled with its scale.

steps.why: Two names are correct at two different scales, so saying which is which shows the distinction was understood.
common_mistakes: Writing both names with no label. Norman Borlaug is the worldwide answer; label M. S. Swaminathan as the Father of the green revolution in India.
Naming a different scientist. Borlaug worldwide, Swaminathan in India.
steps.memory_tip: Borlaug for the world, Swaminathan for India.
